summary: Describes CCNinfo, an experimental tool for Content-Centric Networks that discovers routing path information per name prefix, round-trip time between forwarder and consumer, and the state of in-network caches. It is meant to help understand and debug testbeds and other experimental CCN deployments.

plainLanguage.summary: In a content-centric network, a request travels by content name rather than by address, so the usual traceroute does not show where it went. CCNinfo is a diagnostic that walks the same path the request would take, has each router leave a note saying it passed by, and brings those notes back with the state of the router's cache.

how to discover cache state in content-centric networks
what is the round-trip time to cached content
subtitle: Discovering the path and the cache state of a content name inside a content-centric network.

tldr.problem: In a content-centric network, the operator wants to know which routers a name travels through and what each router has cached, but IP traceroute cannot follow name prefix paths and does not reveal cache state.
tldr.mechanism: CCNinfo defines a Request message that routers add their own Report block to as it travels toward the publisher, and a Reply message that comes back the same way carrying the cache statistics.
tldr.outcome: The reply gives the node identifiers along the path, the number of hops, the round-trip time, and the cache size, object count, access count and lifetime per name prefix, subject to per-router policy.

today: RFC 9344 is an Experimental RFC and has not been obsoleted or updated. The document states that it represents the consensus of the Information-Centric Networking Research Group, that it is not an IETF product and not a standard, and that CCNinfo is intended as an experimental tool for CCNx-based networks.

sections.title: Finding the Path and the Cache
sections.content:
In Content-Centric Networks, publishers provide the content through the network and receivers retrieve it by name. In this architecture, routers forward content requests through their Forwarding Information Bases, which are populated by name-based routing protocols, and CCN also enables receivers to retrieve content from an in-network cache.

While consumers do not generally need to know the content forwarder transmitting the content to them, operators and developers may want to identify the content forwarder and observe the routing path information per name prefix for troubleshooting or investigating network conditions.

IP traceroute is useful for discovering routing conditions in IP networks because it provides intermediate router addresses along the path and the round-trip time for the path. It cannot trace the name prefix paths used in CCN, and it does not obtain the states of the in-network cache.

Contrace enables end users to investigate path and in-network cache conditions in CCN. It is implemented as an external daemon process running over TCP/IP that can interact with a previous CCNx forwarding daemon to retrieve caching information. This solution is flexible, but it requires defining common APIs for global deployment. ICN ping and traceroute are lightweight operational tools that enable a user to explore the paths that reach a publisher or a cache storing the named content, but they do not expose detailed information about the forwarders deployed by a network operator.

This document specifies CCNinfo, an active networking tool for discovering the path and content-caching information in CCN. It defines the protocol messages used to investigate path and in-network cache conditions, and is embedded in the CCNx forwarding process. The Request and Reply messages are encoded in the CCNx TLV format (RFC 8609). The Request-and-Reply message flow, walking up the tree from a consumer toward a publisher, is similar to the behavior of the IP multicast traceroute facility (RFC 8487).

CCNinfo facilitates the tracing of a routing path and provides the round-trip time between the content forwarder and the consumer, the states of the in-network cache per name prefix, and the routing path information per name prefix. It also identifies cache states such as the size of cached Content Objects, the number of cached Content Objects, the number of accesses per content, and the elapsed cache time and remaining cache lifetime of the content.

CCNinfo supports multipath forwarding: Request messages can be forwarded to multiple neighbor routers, and the different Reply messages then come back from different routers or publishers. It also implements policy-based information provisioning, which lets administrators hide secure or private information without disrupting message forwarding. The document represents the consensus of the Information-Centric Networking Research Group and is not an IETF product or a standard.
sections.plainLanguage: In a content-centric network, a request travels by content name rather than by address, so the usual traceroute does not show where it went. CCNinfo is a diagnostic that walks the same path the request would take, has each router leave a note saying it passed by, and brings those notes back with the state of the router's cache.

sections.title: The CCNinfo Message Formats
sections.content:
CCNinfo Request and Reply messages are encoded in the CCNx TLV format. The Request message consists of a fixed header, a Request block TLV and Report block TLVs. The Reply message consists of a fixed header, the Request block TLV, Report block TLVs, a Reply block TLV and Reply sub-block TLVs.

In the fixed header, the PacketType values are PT_CCNINFO_REQUEST and PT_CCNINFO_REPLY, with values 0x03 and 0x04 alongside PT_INTEREST 0x00, PT_CONTENT 0x01 and PT_RETURN 0x02. The messages are forwarded in a hop-by-hop manner. When a Request message reaches the content forwarder, the content forwarder turns it into a Reply message by changing the Type field value in the fixed header and forwards it back toward the node that initiated the Request.

The fixed header also carries a HopLimit of 8 bits, decremented by 1 before the Request packet is forwarded, with the packet discarded if it reaches zero. The HopLimit limits how far a Request may travel and is set by the CCNinfo user program. The ReturnCode field of 8 bits is used for the Reply; until the content forwarder replaces it, it MUST be transmitted as zeros and ignored on receipt. The values are NO_ERROR 0x00, WRONG_IF 0x01, INVALID_REQUEST 0x02, NO_ROUTE 0x03, NO_INFO 0x04, NO_SPACE 0x05, INFO_HIDDEN 0x06, ADMIN_PROHIB 0x0E, UNKNOWN_REQUEST 0x0F and FATAL_ERROR 0x80.

At the outermost level of the payload there is a top-level TLV of type T_DISCOVERY, whose value is 0x0005. The Request header block TLV, of type T_DISC_REQHDR with value 0x0008, sits in the hop-by-hop header because it may change from hop to hop. It carries a 16-bit Request ID used to detect duplicate or delayed Reply messages, a 4-bit SkipHop count, and 12 bits of Flags, of which four are assigned: C selects path discovery or path and cache information, O selects any content forwarder or publisher discovery only, F selects a full discovery request, and V selects reply validation.

The Request block TLV, of type T_DISC_REQ with value 0x000D, is encoded in the payload. It carries a 32-bit Request Arrival Time, a 32-bit NTP timestamp of when the Request arrived at the router, and a variable-length Node Identifier. Each upstream router inserts its own Report block TLV, of type T_DISC_REPORT with value 0x0009, into the hop-by-hop header, carrying the same two fields.

The Reply block TLV, of type T_DISC_REPLY with value 0x000E, is an envelope in the payload for the Reply sub-block TLVs. A Reply sub-block carries eight 32-bit fields: Object Size, the total size in KB of the unexpired Content Objects, with a maximum of about 4.29 TB; Object Count, the number of unexpired Content Objects, at most about 4.29 billion; the number of received Interests; the First and Last sequence numbers; the Elapsed Cache Time in seconds; and the Remaining Cache Lifetime in seconds. Its type is T_DISC_CONTENT 0x0000 when a content forwarder replies with cache information, or T_DISC_CONTENT_PUBLISHER 0x0001 when a first-hop router attached to a publisher replies with the original content information. A router that cannot report one of these values, or does not report it because of policy, MUST set the field to all ones, 0xFFFFFFFF, and the CCNinfo user program MUST report those values as invalid.
sections.plainLanguage: The request and the reply are ordinary CCNx packets with extra blocks added. Each router that handles the request appends a small block recording the time it arrived and its own name. The final reply carries the cache numbers: how many objects are stored, how big they are, how many requests they have served, and how long they have been there and how long they will stay.

sections.title: Router Behavior
sections.content:
A router that receives a CCNinfo Request may first check whether the request came from a valid CCNinfo user, and should terminate it if the sender's signature is invalid. It may also check that the message came from a valid adjacent neighbor, and should silently ignore it if not.

After accepting the request, the router treats HopLimit and SkipHop as counters decremented at each hop. If the HopLimit is zero, or if the SkipHop value is equal to or more than the HopLimit value, the router terminates the request. Otherwise, until SkipHop reaches zero, the router forwards the request to its upstream routers without adding its own Report block and without replying. If the router does not know the upstream routers for the specified name prefix, it terminates the request.

The router then examines the Flags. If the C flag is not set, the request is a routing path information discovery; if it is set, it is a cache information discovery; and if the O flag is set, it is a publisher discovery. For the first two cases, the router examines its FIB and its Content Store. If it caches the specified content, it sends a Reply with its own Reply block and sub-blocks; if there is no room for them, it terminates the request with NO_SPACE. If it does not cache the content but knows the upstream routers, it creates a PIT entry, inserts its own Report block in the hop-by-hop header, and forwards the request. For a publisher discovery, the router checks whether it is the first-hop router for the requested content and replies accordingly.

When forwarding a Request with its Report block, the router records the F flag and the Request ID in the Request block at the corresponding PIT entry, so it can later forward the Reply messages back correctly. When it decides to reply, it inserts a Report block with its arrival time and node identifier, inserts the Reply sub-blocks into the payload, changes the fixed header type from PT_CCNINFO_REQUEST to PT_CCNINFO_REPLY, and forwards the message back hop by hop.

For the full discovery request, the upstream routers simultaneously forward the requests to all of their upstream routers based on their FIBs, so that the user can trace all possible forwarding paths. The PIT entries created by a full discovery request remain until the configured CCNinfo Reply Timeout expires, so that several Reply messages can come back. When the user does not set the F flag, intermediate routers remove the PIT entry as soon as they forward the corresponding Reply. CCNinfo Replies MUST NOT be cached in routers.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router decides what to do with the request: answer it if it holds the content, otherwise pass it on and add a note about itself. The reply then travels back down the same chain of routers, each one forwarding it using the entry it recorded when the request passed through.

sections.title: What the CCNinfo User Gets
sections.content:
A CCNinfo user invokes a program such as the ccninfo command, which creates a CCNinfo Request message and sends it to the user's adjacent neighbor routers of interest. The user later obtains both the routing path information and the in-network cache information in a single Reply.

The program MUST insert the Request ID and the Node Identifier into the Request block, and the Request ID MUST be unique for that user until the corresponding Reply messages are received or the request times out. A user may also require the request to be validated and append its signature into the CCNx ValidationPayload TLV, which a router then checks before forwarding.

After sending the request, and until the reply times out, the program MUST keep the HopLimit, the Request ID and Flags, and the Node Identifier and Request Arrival Time. When a Reply arrives, the program MUST compare the kept Request ID and Node Identifier to identify the matching request and reply; if they do not match, the Reply MUST be silently discarded. If the number of Report blocks in the received Reply is more than the initial HopLimit, the Reply MUST be silently ignored.

A routing path request yields the node identifiers of the intermediate routers, the node identifier of the content forwarder, the number of hops between the content forwarder and the consumer, and the round-trip time between them, per name prefix. A cache information request yields the size of cached Content Objects, the number of them, the number of accesses per content, and the lifetime and expiration time of the cached Content Objects.

The content name may be given either as a prefix name without a chunk number, such as ccnx:/news/today, which returns summary information about the matched Content Objects in the content forwarder, or as an exact name such as ccnx:/news/today/Chunk=10, which returns information only about that Content Object. A Request message MUST NOT be sent with only the scheme name, ccnx:/; it will be rejected and discarded by routers.

The document also lists what can be worked out from the results: the number of hops and the round-trip time, the identity of caching routers, the hop limit needed for the content to reach the consumer, the propagation and queuing delays if the routers have synchronized clocks, the path stretch given as the hop count of the data over the hop count from the consumer to the publisher, and the cache hit probability from the number of received Interests per cache or chunk.
sections.plainLanguage: One command gives back a list of the routers on the path, how many hops away the content is, how long the round trip took, and what each router is holding. You can name a whole prefix to see the summary, or one exact object to see the detail.

sections.title: Configuration and Access Control
sections.content:
The CCNinfo Reply Timeout value is used to time out a Reply. It can be statically configured by a router's administrators and operators. The default value is 3 seconds, and the value SHOULD NOT be larger than 4 seconds and SHOULD NOT be lower than 2 seconds.

If a CCNinfo user does not specify a HopLimit, it is set to 32. A HopLimit of 0 is an invalid request. A router MAY configure valid or invalid networks to enable access control, and the access control MAY be defined per name prefix, such as who can retrieve which name prefix.

The command-line options mirror these settings. The r option gives the number of traced routers and is set in the HopLimit field, so that only that many routers along the path examine their path and cache information. The s option gives the number of skipped routers and is set in the SkipHop field, so that that many upstream routers only forward the request without appending their Report blocks and without sending replies, despite having the corresponding cache. The v option enables the user to validate the request message with their signature, putting it in the CCNx ValidationPayload TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two knobs worth knowing. The hop limit says how far along the path the request should travel, and the skip count says how many routers to pass without asking for their details. There is also a timeout that decides how long a router waits for the reply before giving up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
CCNinfo gives excellent troubleshooting cues, but some administrators may not want to disclose everything about their network to the public, or may wish to transmit private information only to specific members of their network. CCNinfo therefore provides policy-based information provisioning, allowing administrators to specify a response policy for each router.

For who is allowed to retrieve, routers holding the specified content may examine the signature enclosed in the Request and decide whether to disclose content information. If they decide not to, they MUST send the Reply with the ReturnCode of ADMIN_PROHIB and without appending any Reply block or sub-block TLVs. For what kind of cache information, the permission is All, Partial or Deny, defined at the routers. In every case the router does not disrupt the forwarding of the Request and Reply messages: when the ReturnCode is NO_ERROR the router SHOULD insert the Report block, the Node Identifier in it MAY be all zeros according to policy, but the Request Arrival Time SHOULD NOT be null, and the router SHOULD forward the request upstream.

A router MAY filter out requests from invalid CCNinfo users, for example using a list of allowed or disallowed networks. A request from a disallowed network MUST NOT be processed, and the Reply with the ReturnCode of INFO_HIDDEN SHOULD be used to note it, with rate-limited logging of such events possible. CCNinfo can also be used to discover actively used topologies and the type of content being sent by publishers, so if that information is a secret, requests SHOULD be restricted at the border of the domain with the ADMIN_PROHIB return code.

CCNinfo may impose heavy tasks on content forwarders, because they have to look up their internal cache state to report it. The specification allows null values for several fields such as the sequence numbers and the elapsed cache time, so a forwarder can skip the complex functions that would compute them.

On denial of service: a longer Reply Timeout gives an attacker an attractive target against PIT memory, and with the full discovery request several Reply messages may be returned and cause a response storm. Routers MAY configure a shorter timeout, but if it is too short the user receives only partial path information. Routers MAY rate-limit requests by randomly ignoring some consecutive messages, and MAY rate-limit replies in the traced path, in both cases without returning an error message. Finally, the CCNx message format does not define a secure way to verify node adjacency, so hop-by-hop authentication is needed for that.
sections.plainLanguage: The tool can reveal a lot about a network, so each router decides what it is willing to disclose and to whom. It can refuse outright, or answer with the path but leave out the cache details. It can also slow down or ignore repeated requests so that the tool cannot be used to overload the network.

viz.caption: A CCNINFO REQUEST WALKING UP AND THE REPLY WALKING BACK

messages.label: REQUEST
messages.note: The user starts the trace and names the content.

messages.label: REQUEST + REPORT A
messages.note: Router A appends its arrival time and node identifier.

messages.label: REQUEST + REPORT A + REPORT B
messages.note: Router B does the same and forwards upstream.

messages.label: REPLY
messages.note: The forwarder changes the packet type and adds the cache figures.

messages.label: REPLY WITH ALL REPORTS
messages.note: The reply travels back down the pending interest table entries.

viz.caption: THE FIXED HEADER OF A CCNINFO MESSAGE (RFC 9344 FIGURE 4)

fields.name: PacketType
fields.desc: 0x03 for a CCNinfo Request, 0x04 for a CCNinfo Reply.

fields.name: HopLimit
fields.desc: Hops the request may still travel. It is decremented before each forwarding and the packet is discarded at zero.

fields.name: ReturnCode
fields.desc: Set by the content forwarder when the request is turned into a reply; transmitted as zeros until then.

fields.name: Reserved (MBZ)
fields.desc: Transmitted as zeros and ignored on receipt.

items.label: WRONG_IF
items.desc: The request arrived on an interface the router would not use for the name.

items.label: NO_ROUTE
items.desc: The router has no route for the name prefix.

items.label: NO_INFO
items.desc: The router has no cache information for the name prefix.

items.label: NO_SPACE
items.desc: There was not enough room to insert another Report block.

items.label: INFO_HIDDEN
items.desc: Information is hidden from this discovery owing to policy.

items.label: FATAL_ERROR
items.desc: A fatal error, such as a routing loop in the Request blocks.
